title: Deep Equilibrium Models

citations.claim: Bai et al. proposed the deep equilibrium model (DEQ), which directly finds the fixed point of a weight-tied transformation via root-finding rather than iteratively stacking layers, effectively representing an infinite-depth network.
DEQ enables backpropagation through the equilibrium point using implicit differentiation, requiring only constant memory regardless of the effective depth of the network.
Bai et al. demonstrated that DEQ can achieve up to 88% memory reduction compared to conventional deep networks while maintaining competitive performance on large-scale language modeling tasks.
DEQ uses Broyden's method, a quasi-Newton approach, to efficiently approximate the inverse Jacobian during both forward and backward passes, avoiding the cubic cost of direct inversion.
Bai et al. proved that stacking multiple DEQs does not create extra representational power over a single DEQ, establishing the universality of single-layer DEQ models.
Weight tying in deep networks acts as a form of regularization that stabilizes training and supports generalization, while significantly reducing the model size.
DEQ was motivated by the observation that the hidden layers of many existing deep sequence models with weight tying converge towards a fixed point as depth increases.
The DEQ approach is independent of the choice of the internal transformation function, and the same memory benefits apply regardless of the type of transformation used.
DEQ can be instantiated with different architectures including trellis networks (weight-tied temporal convolutions) and universal transformers (weight-tied multi-head self-attention).

Unlike ODE-based methods that backpropagate through the entire latent trajectory using the adjoint system, DEQ solves directly for equilibria via quasi-Newton methods and backpropagates through the fixed point without regard for the solution path.

do_not_claim: DEQ was proposed for signal processing or inverse problems (it was proposed for sequence modeling)
DEQ uses algorithm unrolling (it replaces unrolling with direct equilibrium computation)
DEQ was applied to baseline correction or chromatography
DEQ inherently learns per-signal parameters (it learns shared weight-tied transformations)
